title: Part 1
text: Dogfight Chapter 1: Tagging the Predator The trial ended in blood and silence. Hooks stood empty. Survivors bled into the Fog, their screams already dissolving in the distance, as they always did. Wesker stood tall amid the wreckage of smashed pallets and discarded medkits that littered the admin desk of Lery’s, chest heaving — not from exertion, more from restraint. Uroboros still pulsed under his skin like a tethered storm, hungry and writhing. There was often a kind of tension hangover after a match; the bloodlust from the fight never quite bleeding off right away even when there was nothing left to throw, but no good would come of taking it out on the surroundings. Best to just head home and wait it out. He tilted his head, waiting. The Entity should have pulled him by now, tugging him back to the RPD station in that familiar haze of static unraveling. She was taking her time today, it seemed. Not totally unusual; some days the Entity took longer than others to extract her killers, and it really wasn’t often that he got the chance to stretch out in another domain like this. He stilled, every sense straining. Nothing moved. Even the crows were gone. The calm should have been satisfying — a clean hunt, quota met — but the stillness was itching at him regardless, driving him to idly pace the halls while he waited. The halls were gray with dust, the sky out the stained windows a smear of barely visible light. Each footstep came back to him a fraction late, like the echo of a heartbeat out of rhythm. He followed the sound anyway, pacing through the ruin simply because doing nothing felt worse. The air pressed thicker the further he went, heavy with heat. Something sharp lived inside it, a scent vaguely under the rust and rot: copper, antiseptic... sweetness. He took it in, curious, before he realized he shouldn’t have. It burned faintly, a chemical perfume that clung to the back of his throat. He winced, annoyed, and kept moving. The smell followed. He hadn’t noticed it during the hunt, entirely too wrapped up in the angles and vaults to really take in the ambient smell of the center. Now that he had nothing else to focus on, it was everywhere. A prickle crept up his neck. The Fog’s edges shimmered — too bright, too alive. His skin tightened, pupils contracting to pinpoints as Uroboros stirred under his ribs. He felt watched despite the emptiness of the hallways. No matter how hard he listened, there was nothing to sense. He was positive that he was alone. Still, this felt... wrong. He turned once more, scanning the perimeter, but the world looked subtly warped — colors shifting toward a feverish spectrum, shapes sliding where they should have held. His breath hitched, shallow. Heat rippled down his spine. The viral hum inside him spiked in answer, apparently just as restless. He hadn’t gone that much harder than normal this trial, had he? He would need to take a solid rest back at the station, provided the Entity left him be. Excessive fatigue wasn’t unheard of, but it had been a while since he had felt its effects; and he had been running trials back-to-back as of late with very little downtime between. Even a god needed a nap once in a while. Another breath. A sweetness on the air. Sickly-sweet. Something acrid curled in behind it, coating his tongue, dragging a cough up from deep in his chest. If the Fog didn’t take him home soon, he would need to wait out by the gate. Without the blood and bitter terror of the survivors, the institute really was impossible to linger in for long. What was taking Her so long, anyways? The halls were clearly dusted with her Fog, lightly coiling around broken pallets and doorframes, as if it somehow failed to notice he was even there still. His stance shifted. He stretched slightly, one hand lifting to adjust his coat as if warding off the unease, his fingers twitched before they could land. A tremor flickered through his arm, sharp and precise. The air around him moved slightly, a faint hiss like an exhale from the walls, almost polite. He recognized the sound instantly, the realization hitting like a slap. Not fatigue. He had wandered willingly straight into a trap. A second tremor. His foot skidded half a step, as if his leg had forgotten how to obey. The Fog around him thickened, something in his head tilting sharply sideways. His vision warped like light through oil, and a sudden weight pressed behind his eyes. "What—" His body pitched forward, catching himself against a nearby window vault. He drew another breath out of reflex and choked on it. The gas laced deep, threading nerves, short-circuiting synapses. The infection under his skin reacted violently, veins blooming black as it tried to purge the intrusion. His muscles trembled from the internal war. Wesker staggered, one hand braced against the wall, the other trying to ward off further contamination, burying his face in a sleeve. The hiss grew louder, seemingly from every wall now. A chemical cocktail working down into his blood, sneaking past Uroboros’ defenses before the virus could even identify the intrusion. He had wandered too far into the building to get back to the outside air of the gate. The timing had been exact. This wasn’t brute force. It was finesse. A slow bleed. A calculated takedown. “Show yourself!” The snarl broke halfway through, distorted by a spasm that clenched his jaw shut. Gold flared behind his eyes as the virus rose to meet the threat. For a moment he almost held it — the predator forcing the body upright through sheer defiance, every tendon drawn like wire. Then the current screamed through the room, a white- blue arc that swallowed sound and thought alike. Electricity tore through him, bouncing between muscle and bone in a morbid chain reaction. Not raw damage, calibration. A shock tailored for his frame, tuned perfectly to override every fiber of defiance. His spine bowed in an arc as he crashed back against the tile, backlit by flickers of arc-light. Every nerve still screamed, but the body that should have obeyed them didn’t exist for a breathless second. Only pressure. A single, endless tone drilled through his skull while the rest of the world receded partially. He didn’t lose consciousness so much as slide away from it — a slow, drowning descent he fought the entire way. Muscles twitched in defiance, random surges of strength trying to pull him upright. The virus kept firing, desperate to restore order, burning through what oxygen remained. His chest convulsed once, twice. Uncoordinated limbs trying to push him upright, only to find their nerve signals either rerouted or straight up missing. Somewhere above the god-awful ringing through his head, something ticked. Bootsteps, measured and calm. A soft crackle of static answered by the scrape of a metal instrument tray. He couldn’t see through the spots of white and black, vague sharp scents driving through the haze in the few stuttering breaths he managed — ozone, antiseptic, faint alcohol on a gloved hand. His hearing staggered back one layer at a time; first the hiss of air vents, then a voice, blurred by distance but unmistakable in tone. The world tilted in stuttering frames. His vision crawled back by degrees, a film of static peeling off the edges. Cold. Steel walls. Shadows moving with precision instead of panic. The Fog’s usual hum had changed; it carried a rhythm now, electrical, surgical. He forced air into his lungs. It scraped raw, but it came. His hand twitched, scraping against the tile, fingers trying to curl. Move. His muscles spasmed instead, half-fire, half-failure. Uroboros thrashed under the skin, black veins splitting and healing in the same breath. The infection wanted to fight. His body wanted to obey. But the signals were wrong — every nerve fired out of order. A cold fingertip pressed against the inside of his wrist. Counting, clinical. Then a small, pleased hum. “Remarkable," Herman murmured, crouching beside him. "Even subdued, your resistance is impressive. The Fog nearly reclaimed you before I could stabilize the dose." Wesker’s head jerked toward the sound, the motion sending vertigo knifing through him. He caught the briefest shape — the outline of a gas mask, white coat, gleam of metal — and tried to stand anyway. His knees obeyed a moment too late, his own momentum collapsing him forward onto his palms. His body shook with the effort, sweat and blood mingling in neat drops across the floor. “Persistent,” Herman mused, “But predictable.” Wesker forced breath through clenched teeth, lips twitching into a snarl. “You... dare—” Herman stood, baton humming to life with a lazy flick of his thumb. “I do.” The air vibrated. Ozone filled the gap between them. “Stay down,” he advised softly. The next arc landed square across Wesker’s back. White fire. Every muscle seized, diaphragm locked against a pained scream. The current held for a full three seconds. Long enough for the virus to thrash against itself, for his vision to splinter again into black and gold, for strength to become convulsion. When it finally cut, he was on the floor again, chest heaving, body trembling in the aftermath. Nerves sang, muscles flickered in uncoordinated spasms, Uroboros retreating deep into the bone to survive the assault. Herman crouched nearby, studying the aftermath with professional satisfaction. The gloved hand returned to the wrist once more, counting beats. Steady enough now. Controlled. “Even now, the synaptic recovery is extraordinary. You’re actually still aware, aren’t you? Well, I can’t have you getting up too soon.” Herman loomed overhead, fog coiling around his ankles as the baton rose for a final, surgical strike. The blow landed with intent, just enough to make sure Wesker’s next memory would begin somewhere else. White swallowed everything. He surfaced slowly, dragged upward through the sludge of unconsciousness. Sparks still danced behind his eyelids, mingling with a throb through his skull that threatened to take him back under. The chemical tang clung thick in his throat, every breath laced with metal and smoke. His muscles twitched without command — phantom echoes of the shocks that had put him down. When his vision cleared, he wasn’t in the trial. He was sprawled on the cold steel of the station floor. He pushed himself upright with effort, balance wavering. Every muscle felt wrong. Slow. Re-synced. One hand pressed to his head, trying to settle the residual spinning from the toxin that hadn’t quite finished clearing from his system yet. The movement set off a sharp sting in his wrist, as if something had cut into him. His eyes dropped to the offending limb. A sleek, black band, fused around his wrist like a parasite. No latch. No weld. It pulsed faintly against his skin, like it was breathing with him. Or against him. The metal laid flush against his skin, and attempting to rotate it in place sent a sharp stab straight to the bone. The band had teeth, at least some long enough to reach down through muscle, grazing bone and anchoring it in place. Embedded. Wesker curled his fingers, flexing against the band, pulsing his virus against it. Pain. Searing. Sharp. Immediate. Agony punched through him, dropping him to one knee before he could prepare, vision scattering in a haze of static. Overhead, an intercom speaker crackled, the Doctor’s chuckles bleeding through the walls. “Well, now that IS a strong reaction. Let me jot that down.” Wesker snarled at the voice, the intrusion on the only place in this cursed Fog that was his alone. To one side, the faintest movement of a security camera caught in his peripherals as it rotated to find him. “What is this,” his voice low, tight with fury. “What did you do to me?” “Oh, don’t be so dramatic,” Herman cooed. “It’s just a little... observer collar. Nothing too invasive. Think of it as telemetry with perks. It pings. It pricks. It occasionally floods your bloodstream with helpful mood stabilizers. And if you behave... maybe even a treat.” “You’re still free to hunt, of course. Mostly. Just don’t mind the tremors. Or the aim drift. Or the fact that you might forget what you were doing halfway through a chase. It’s all part of the fun. Honestly, you should be grateful. Most specimens don’t get to roam. You’re free-range. Very modern.” Wesker dragged in a breath, chest heaving against the static still caging his ribs. “I will end you.” Herman’s laugh was warm, indulgent. “Oh, I hope so. Otherwise — where’s the fun?” A faint scratch of pen on clipboard followed, his voice dipping into clinical detachment as if Wesker’s rage were nothing more than a lab reading. “Subject 06-W: Successful restraint application. Initial response: extreme hostility. Uroboros activity — suppressed but volatile. Further observation required.” Chapter 2: The First Misfire The Fog unfolded around him, dropping him into the corroded halls of Midwitch. The air smelled of salt, rust, and purpose; steel corridors, slick with condensation, the dull electric hum that meant life. Wesker stepped forward through it, shoulders square, the practiced rhythm of a hunter in his element. Controlled. Familiar. The sting of Herman’s baton, the blackout, the unfamiliar weight at his wrist — all ghosts. Faint echoes. Whatever the Doctor had done, the Fog would bleed it clean. It always had. Here, he was still the killer. Still the apex. He told himself that with every step. And for a few heartbeats, it was even true. A misfired generator flared in the distance. The first chase was a breath away, and he glided toward it, each step clean and confident. Feng darted into view between the pallets, her ponytail snapping like a warning flag. He tracked her automatically — angle, distance, timing. Uroboros surged at his call, pulsing hot and certain through every muscle fiber. He reached for it — And his arm stopped. Not hesitated. Locked. Every muscle from shoulder to wrist seized mid-motion, tendons pulled tight as wire. His lunge faltered, all power diverted into useless momentum. For a split second, his entire system stuttered: vision fractured into white noise, footsteps blurred beneath him. A static heartbeat pounded in his ears. He swiped wide. Feng, shocked for half a breath, twisted out of reach and bolted. Her startled yelp turned into a laugh. It was short, bright, human. Full of the kind of relief that comes with a monster tripping when it should have caught you. She vaulted a pallet and dared a look back. Dared. Wesker's jaw clenched hard enough to ache. He forced movement back into his limbs, teeth grinding as he ripped control back from wherever it had gone. The virus surged in answer, pulsing hot and agitated under the skin — but the pathway it was trying to follow had already been rerouted. Uroboros twisted against the resistance like a living thing but found no foothold. The misfire wasn’t physical. It was command-level. The cuff at his wrist pulsed again — a gentle thrum, almost curious. He caught her eventually. Crushed her to the hook with brutal efficiency, as expected. The hook screamed as it accepted her weight; the Fog purred, sated. But the moment was already gone. The rhythm was wrong. Too slow. Too heavy. Not the clean predator he demanded of himself. As the trial dragged on, the rot set in. A half-second lag on each strike. A stutter in the throws. Muscle memory corrupted. Precision frayed. He felt the precision bleeding out of him with each chase. Somewhere across the map, a locker creaked open. Footsteps danced toward a generator. He followed automatically — but his chest was tight. Not with strain. With uncertainty. He adjusted. He always did. But it wasn’t enough. Every time the cuff warmed against his skin, it left behind a tremor. The next strike came a fraction too slow. The next throw overcorrected. The next lunge landed — but sloppily. A half- second off at every angle. Worse than failure was the realization: he was no longer sure whether the failures were his. Then came the pulse. Mid-trial. No warning. The band warmed gently against the bone, like approval. A pat on the head dripping with condescension. Wesker froze. He was standing in the open. No one nearby. No threat. Nothing to react to. And yet — the cuff had reacted anyways. In the silence between the Fog’s murmurs, a slow coil of unease threaded through him. That pulse had meant something. He was being monitored. Still. Herman was watching. Recording. Adjusting. Chapter 3: Futility The return to his domain was supposed to be automatic, restorative. He should have felt the usual clarity returning, Uroboros smoothing through his veins, mind slotting back into precision. Instead, the stillness of the station almost seemed to hum in a rhythm that matched the pulse under the cuff. Wesker paced like a caged animal, back in the far corner of the RPD station that was supposed to be his. The Fog was quiet here. Too quiet. A stillness that only gave his fury room to breathe and made every joint ache. He dismissed it at first. The body always complained after a hunt. He washed the blood from his gloves, reset the equipment, sat at the edge of a bench and waited for the fatigue to bleed away. It didn’t. The band at his wrist warmed by degrees; barely perceptible at first, then sharp enough to feel like a fever under the skin. He flexed his hand, irritation a slow rise in his throat. Fine. He would catalogue the sensation, adapt. His eyes stayed fixed on the black band clamped to his wrist. The faint hum never stopped. A constant presence: an incessant, pulsing reminder that it was there. Fused deep; bonded like scar tissue. Even when he wasn’t moving, he could feel it breathing with him, the long internal spikes scraping him raw. He tested the edges with the side of a knuckle. The band bit with a tiny electronic flare across bone and tendon — a polite warning that tasted like lightning in his teeth. Somewhere above, the old intercom system clicked once — metallic, empty. Just the soft pop of a microphone live and waiting. He looked up, expression flat. “Doctor.” A snarl wrapped in civility. No answer. He meandered through the hallway slowly. At the doorway to the locker room, the cuff pulsed again — one quick shock that wasn’t pain so much as intrusion, a shiver that scraped the edge of every nerve. He staggered a half step before catching himself on the frame. “Childish.” He rubbed the wrist until sensation returned. The speakers exhaled a whisper of static, like the sound of breath filtered through glass. The quiet reasserted itself; the hum dropped away. He lowered himself to a bench, unwilling to show how much the jolt had burned. When he finally let his eyes close, the band cooled, almost gentle. For a few breaths he almost believed the experiment had paused. A low hiss: a faint pneumatic sigh under the metal. It wasn’t enough to cripple — just a drift of cold through the veins, a chemical whisper that left his thoughts too sharp and his body too heavy. A cheeky denial of rest. Wesker inhaled through the sensation, anger rolling up through him slow and black. This intrusion on his life had gone on long enough. Trying for a more subtle approach, he tried to work the virus under his skin as a wedge; to have Uroboros pry at the connection from within. The infection liked to be useful; it liked resistance. For a second he felt the tiniest give — a microscopic loosening in the cuff’s adhesive bite — and his heart stuttered at the thought of finally getting leverage as he pushed harder. Uroboros responded instantly, veins bulging as oily tendrils writhed up under the skin. The virus coiled around the band like a serpent, lashing at the flush-seated metal, bubbling where it touched — but each strike ended in recoil. It couldn’t grip. Couldn’t burn. Couldn’t bite. He snarled. Again. Harder. The infection swelled, pushing heat and pressure into the wrist until the skin trembled with strain. The band retaliated not with brute force but with bureaucracy. A soft injection hissed under the cuff edge — a gust of cool fluid, a bitter chemical bloom that stabbed at his vision and left organs humming with the taste of copper and bile. The cuff’s micro-sensors read the change and closed within milliseconds, a calibrated clamp that tightened an internal cycle of small, escalating shocks and a nausea-inducing cascade of neuromodulators. The world tipped sideways, stomach reeling from the assault even as his virus ate through the chemicals. He turned, grabbed his combat knife from the locker bench, and pressed the tip against the faintest ghost of a seam in the band — a trick of the light, maybe. Hopefully, just enough. The cuff sparked red. The shock tore down his arm, a precision strike against the nerves that set his heart lurching unsteadily against his ribs. The knife jumped from his fingers with a clatter, hand spasming so violently it left his wrist half-numb. Uroboros hissed inward like steam into a vacuum, retreating from the bone as if it had been scalded. He’d never be able to hold the combat knife steady enough to try again, not with how hard his hand vibrated from the aftershock. He glared at the band, breathing heavier now. The band had progressed from a mere insult to an outright challenge. He braced the wrist against the edge of the bench and tried again, bare fingers scrabbling against the edge of the metal. The pain came instantly this time, a punishment for his efforts. It stabbed through tendon and muscle, a sharp, surgical burn that left him grinding his teeth just to stay upright. Uroboros flared again in pure defiance, flooding up his arm, trying again to swell beneath it and force it loose. It couldn’t cling. Couldn’t anchor. It slipped off and recoiled again with a ripple of pain that shot down through his ribcage. The backlash rattled his spine. Still, he kept going. Dug his thumb in, tried to wedge under it. Nothing. Tried to pull. Nothing. He rotated his wrist to the edge of the locker frame and slammed it once — then again. Then again. Metal shrieked and dented in. Skin split. Bone cracked. Blood smeared the frame. The Fog shifted, the injuries vanishing like they had never been there in the first place. The cuff remained untouched. He dropped to a knee, growling through the hurt, one hand braced against the wall, vision tunneling away from the sensation. For the first time in years, brute force had failed him completely. He straightened slowly, breathing through clenched teeth. The band glowed faintly with heat, offering consequences he had no counter for in the moment. He could try to knife his way under it, tissue damage be damned, but every metal undercut carried the risk of electronic lash and organ-straining bio-doses. There was no doubt anymore — even if he tried to remove the wrist entirely, the Fog would just grow it back. The station wasn’t his safe space anymore. He was never off duty now. And Herman was watching. The realization hit like a second blow: this wasn’t just restraint. It was ownership. A leash around his instincts. Around his choices. Around his life. He may as well have been back under Spencer’s thumb — a weapon in a glass box. But at least Spencer had been mortal. Predictable. Manipulable. This lunatic was something else entirely. Smarter. Bolder. And worse of all: amused. Wesker had been played. Expertly. Precisely. And he would never forgive it. When he tested his hand again, the band flared in a small, punitive pulse. He tasted metal, but did not flinch. Chapter 4: Breaking Point He was eventually called to another trial, not that he ever had much say in the matter. The Fog spilled open, and Wesker moved like a blade in a shaking hand — sharp, but not steady. The cuff’s hum had threaded itself into the rhythm of his steps, each pulse tightening its hold. The first down came clumsily. Nea, screaming, kicking, was already hoisted in his grasp when the band flared red. His grip shattered open, tendons convulsing in painful stutters. She hit the ground running before he could force his body back into motion. A heartbeat later, the shockwave came — numb at first, then razor-sharp, crawling down his arm and shorting out his vision with static bursts and harsh glaring lights. By the time he blinked it clear, she was gone. And they had all noticed. Dwight body-blocked at a doorway, something he never would’ve dared before. Wesker’s lunge carried wide, nearly tripping over the man as the window missed entirely. Jake baited a strike at a pallet and ducked away a second early — timing gambled, timing won — as the wood splintered against Wesker’s shoulder. Even Claudette, usually cautious to the point of paranoia, took bolder paths. The more he missed, the more brazen they became. And when he did manage to hit, they didn’t flinch. They regrouped quickly, pulled each other up with the ease of a practiced routine. No panic. No fear. They didn’t know what was wrong. They didn’t need to. All they knew was that the killer who once carved clean through trials now moved in fits and fractures. The match ended with too many survivors upright, their laughter bleeding faint through the Fog as it closed. Wesker stood frozen in the haze, jaw tight, lungs burning. The cuff's glow sank back to its usual throb — unassuming, present, mocking. They weren’t afraid anymore. They were testing him. The next trial pushed him to the edge. By mid-match, every swing felt ragged. The static in his head came in waves now, crashing over him seemingly at random. His body staggered on inputs he never meant to send. Precision bled away in stutters. Hooks passed without use. Grabs slipped without purchase. His kills dropped. Quota dropped. The survivors began to play with him. Taunting loops. Bold saves. Close passes behind his back. Jake laughed out loud when a fully charged lunge crumpled into a twitching fall, dropping Wesker to one knee with a frustrated snarl. He abandoned the chase before the gates even fully powered up. He staggered into a deserted corridor of the realm, back braced against the wall, clutching the cuff until his knuckles went white, trying to will the world around him to settle. His breaths came harsh and uneven. Uroboros flared under the skin — eager, aggressive — but recoiled instantly as it brushed the device. The cuff answered in kind, sending a jolt down his arm that stole the strength from his legs. He dropped hard to the floor, gasping as the current burned down through his spine. His chest seized in painful staccato, breath coming shallow and uneven, rhythm knocked askew. Vision spun in swirls of too bright light that sent bursts of nausea through his core. Static crawled the walls. And somewhere, unseen, Herman marked another note. Footsteps. Too cautious to be chasing. Too slow to be fleeing. Hesitation written into the weight of each step. "...Wesker?" Shaky, soft. Open concern. Someone who knew what a stupid idea it was to come this close. Someone who should have known better but couldn’t help himself. He loitered a ways out of reach, visible only in glimpses: the gleam of glasses, the way his hands refused to lower the flashlight. The Fairfield kid. Figures. Wesker didn’t lift his head, but the tension in his frame coiled tighter. He gripped the cuff tighter, breath hissing into a low snarl. Dwight’s silhouette edged into view — half-crouched, cautious, as if approaching a wounded predator that might still bite. He hovered just down the corridor now, clearly second-guessing his life choices, but still moving forward one trembling step at a time. “You’ve been... off lately,” Dwight ventured at last. “Kind of a nice change of pace, but...you don’t seem... I just... look, are you okay?” He meant it. The idiot meant it. Wesker didn’t even need to see his face to know what that look held — sympathy. Pity. The audacity of concern. It detonated something inside him. Wesker moved before he could think, lunging across the space like a sprung trap. Dwight barely had time to gasp before he was slammed against the wall, Wesker’s hand at his throat, the other crushing down on his shoulder. "You dare to look at me like that?!" Dwight choked, hands scrabbling uselessly at the arm restraining him, boots scraping for footing against the tile, but Wesker barely noticed. The cuff’s glow flared red between them. Dwight’s gaze dropped instinctively to it — face blanching, confusion mingling with dawning fear. The cuff flared again, sparks dancing over the band, firing a pulse like a hammer blow. Wesker’s whole body jerked with it, the pain flaring down his spine and locking his joints. His grip faltered, arms twitching involuntarily. Dwight dropped to the floor, coughing as he scrambled down the hall and out of reach. Either he was extremely lucky, or something was seriously wrong. Wesker just had him, and something stronger than Wesker had forced him to let go. Wesker didn’t chase. He couldn’t. His hands spasmed uselessly at his sides, and all he could do was snarl through gritted teeth as Dwight vanished into the Fog, fear and something dangerously close to understanding in his eyes. He pressed his forehead to cold stone, forcing breath through his teeth into failing lungs. Every muscle ached, every nerve felt raw. The Entity’s
